deep_dive_html:
The Hidden Costs of Broad Maintenance Definitions

For salon owners, the Common Area Maintenance (CAM) clause is often a silent profit killer. Unlike standard retail, salons operate with high-intensity utility usage and specific plumbing and HVAC requirements. Landlords frequently draft CAM provisions that are intentionally broad, allowing them to pass through costs for building-wide capital improvements or excessive administrative fees under the guise of general maintenance. If your lease lacks a clear distinction between controllable and uncontrollable expenses, you may find yourself subsidizing the landlord's long-term structural investments.

The primary danger lies in the unspecified repairs trap. A landlord might include all necessary repairs to the building's plumbing and electrical systems within the CAM budget. For a salon, a single leak in a shared line could trigger a massive, unbudgeted expense passed directly to you. Furthermore, many landlords attempt to apply a percentage-based administrative fee on top of all CAM expenses, effectively charging you a premium to manage their own property.

Establishing Market-Standard Protections

To protect your salon's margins, you must move away from gross CAM structures and toward highly defined, capped obligations. A sophisticated lease should clearly delineate between expenses the landlord can control—such as landscaping, janitorial services, and security—and those they cannot, such as property taxes and insurance. The following protections are non-negotiable for high-impact tenants:

  • Controllable Expense Caps: Limiting the annual increase of controllable CAM to a fixed percentage such as three to five percent.
  • Capital Expenditure Exclusions: Ensuring that structural repairs, such as roof replacements or parking lot repaving, are excluded from the annual CAM budget.
  • Audit Rights: Explicitly reserving the right to inspect the landlord's books and records to verify the accuracy of CAM reconciliations.
  • Administrative Fee Limits: Capping the landlord's management fee at a fixed, reasonable percentage of the total CAM spend.
